title: Life on a grid
interaction: Paint a few squares on a grid and press step: every square counts its live neighbours at once, and the three rules (lonely dies, crowded dies, exactly three neighbours gives birth) show as the counts on each square. Press play and find the shapes that blink, the ones that sit still and the glider that walks across the board. Change one number in a rule and watch the same seed grow, freeze or die.
takeaway: A rule about counting neighbours, applied to every square at once, makes things that blink, walk and grow that nobody drew.
pitfall: All squares update together from the previous picture, not one after another; a page that updates in place gets wrong patterns. And do not call Life 'random': the same seed gives the same future every time.
why: Numberphile, 'Inventing Game of Life (John Conway)' (title confirmed; YouTube does not render view counts in fetch); promotes the Reserve item 'Cellular automata' at level 0. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R9Plq-D1gEk
overlapWith: chaos-fractals (level 2) shows simple rules making unpredictable paths; this page's rule is three neighbour counts on a grid the reader paints, and the reader can edit the rule.

title: A picture is a grid of numbers
interaction: Pinch into a photograph until it breaks into squares, then into one square: a single colour, kept as three counts. Paint a tiny picture on a grid of lights that are only on or off and read the row of numbers that describes it; switch to four shades of grey, then to colour, and the row of numbers grows. Double the grid's size and watch the picture sharpen while the number count jumps fourfold.
takeaway: A picture in a computer is a grid of squares each kept as a few numbers, so more squares mean a sharper picture and four times as many numbers for each doubling.
needs: One small photograph, CC0 from Wikimedia Commons or taken in-house.
pitfall: Zooming in does not add detail: a blurry photo enlarged stays blurry, which the page shows instead of the TV trope of 'enhance'. Keep to counts; no bits, bytes or hex.
why: England KS3 computing: 'how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally'; CS Unplugged's Image Representation ('Colour by Numbers') activity. https://classic.csunplugged.org/activities/image-representation/
overlapWith: binary (level 1) reads one byte as a colour among other conventions; this page never shows a bit, only the grid, the shade counts and the resolution.
needsSource: A CC0 photograph from Wikimedia Commons, or an in-house photo; no model or dataset.

title: Repeat: loops
interaction: Draw a square by giving a pen-robot eight cards, then wrap 'forward, turn' in a repeat card set to 4 and get the same square from two cards; the page counts cards written against steps taken. Change the repeat count and the turn and the square becomes a triangle, a hexagon, a star. Put a repeat inside a repeat and a few cards draw a flower of forty squares.
takeaway: A loop does the same few steps many times, so a handful of cards can draw a picture of thousands of steps, and changing one number changes the whole picture.
pitfall: The turn for a star is the robot's own turn, not the star's inside angle; let the reader see a wrong count fail to close the shape rather than correcting it.
why: England KS2 computing: 'use sequence, selection, and repetition in programs; work with variables and various forms of input and output'. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study
overlapWith: cpu (level 2) runs a loop as a conditional jump over machine instructions; here the loop is a card that wraps other cards, with no counters or jumps shown.

title: A robot follows instructions
interaction: Drag instruction cards (forward, turn left, turn right, pick up) into a list and press run: a robot on a floor grid does exactly what the cards say, in order, and walks into the wall if that is what they say. Fix the list until it reaches the flag, then try the 'make a sandwich' list with a step missing and watch the robot butter the air. Hand the same list to a second robot standing somewhere else and see where it ends up.
takeaway: A robot does exactly what its list says, in order, nothing more and nothing less, so a missing or swapped card changes the whole result.
pitfall: The computer does not 'understand' the goal: a list that nearly works gets no credit, and the page must never auto-correct the reader's list. Also, left and right are the robot's, not the viewer's.
why: England KS1 computing: 'programs execute by following precise and unambiguous instructions'; CS Unplugged Kidbots (ages 5 to 10). https://www.csunplugged.org/en/topics/kidbots/
overlapWith: cpu (level 2) steps a real processor through fetch, decode and execute with registers and memory; this page has a robot and cards, no memory or arithmetic, and is the first idea of a program.

title: Screens and pixels
interaction: Pinch into a photo until the picture falls apart into a grid of squares, then further, until each square turns out to be three tiny lights, red, green and blue, side by side. Pick one square and slide its three lights up and down: from a distance the square turns yellow, pink, white or black, with no yellow or white light anywhere in it. Then take pixels away from the whole picture, by halves, and watch a face become blocks.
takeaway: A screen picture is a grid of tiny red, green and blue lights, and every colour you see on it is those three lights at different brightnesses, blurred together by your eye.
needs: One photograph under CC0 (Wikimedia Commons), shown at its real pixel grid.
needsSource: none beyond a CC0 photograph; the subpixel drawing and the mixing are computed from the pixel values.
pitfall: There is no yellow or white light on the screen: white is all three lights on. A black pixel is lights off, or on an LCD a backlight blocked by a shutter; say which kind of screen is drawn rather than presenting one as how all screens work.
why: England KS3 computing: 'understand how data of various types (including text, sounds and pictures) can be represented and manipulated digitally, in the form of binary digits' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study).
overlapWith: vision-color: that page mixes red, green and blue light to match a colour and shows the cone responses; this one starts from the object, the screen, and shows that the mixing is done by three tiny lights per pixel and the grid they make, with no eye model.

title: Secret codes & code-breaking
interaction: Turn the inner ring of a code wheel and type a message: each letter steps along the alphabet by the same amount, and your friend turns the ring back to read it. A spy who does not know the turn tries all 25 turns at once and the one that reads as words jumps out. Scramble the alphabet instead of turning it; now the spy counts the letters in the secret message, lines its tallest bar up with the tallest bar of ordinary English, and the message comes out letter by letter.
takeaway: A code that shifts every letter the same way falls to trying all 25 shifts, and a code that scrambles the alphabet falls to counting letters, because E stays the most common letter however it is disguised.
needs: English letter frequencies counted at build time by a script from a public-domain text, e.g. Project Gutenberg's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (public domain), not typed in from memory.
pitfall: A short message has too few letters for counting to work: show the counting fail on a one-line note and succeed on a paragraph, rather than pretending frequency analysis always works.
why: The National Cipher Challenge, the University of Southampton's codebreaking competition for school teams, starts every year with ciphers of this kind. https://www.cipherchallenge.org/
overlapWith: cryptography (level 2) covers key exchange, hashing and signatures with modular arithmetic; this page is pen-and-paper ciphers and the two ways they break, with no keys shared over a channel.
needsSource: A Project Gutenberg public-domain English text for the letter counts.

title: Solving a maze
interaction: Press 'new maze' and the page draws one; put your explorer's hand on the right-hand wall and press walk: it traces every dead end and comes out at the exit. Switch to a maze with an island in it and watch the same explorer circle the island forever. Give it chalk to mark every passage it enters and it finds the way out of any maze; then compare its chalk marks with the shortest route.
takeaway: Keeping one hand on the wall gets you out of a maze without loops but circles forever when there is an island, while an explorer that marks where it has been always gets out.
pitfall: The wall-follower fails on mazes that are not simply connected (loops, islands) and when started from inside; the marking explorer finds an exit but not necessarily the shortest route: show both limits.
why: Wikipedia, 'Maze-solving algorithm' (wall follower; Trémaux's algorithm, which 'is not guaranteed to find the shortest route'). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maze-solving_algorithm
overlapWith: graph-search (level 1) expands breadth-first and A* frontiers on a grid with costs; this page sends one explorer with one rule and never shows a frontier or a cost.

title: A sorting machine
interaction: Six numbered balls roll down a board of tracks; where two tracks meet, the smaller ball goes left and the larger right, and the balls arrive at the bottom in order. Rebuild the board yourself by placing meeting points, drop a shuffled set of balls and see whether they come out sorted; press 'try every order' and the page drops all 720 shuffles and reports any that fail. Then count how many meeting points fire at the same moment: the board sorts in rounds, not one swap at a time.
takeaway: A fixed board of pairwise swaps sorts any shuffle of the balls, and several swaps happen at once, so the board finishes in fewer rounds than it has swaps.
pitfall: A board that sorts the examples you tried may still fail on another order; the page must test all orders, not a few. And this is not how most software sorts: say it is how hardware and parallel sorters do it.
why: CS Unplugged Sorting Networks, with lessons for ages 5 to 7, 8 to 10 and 11 to 14 (site content CC BY-SA 4.0; reuse the idea, not the worksheets). https://www.csunplugged.org/en/topics/sorting-networks/
overlapWith: sorting (level 1) steps bubble, insertion, merge and quick sort one comparison at a time and plots Big-O; this page is a fixed, parallel board of swaps the reader builds and verifies, with no growth curves.

title: Sound as a list of numbers
interaction: Record a clap or a word (or pick a shipped clip) and see it as a wiggly line; a slider sets how many times a second the computer measures the line, from tens of thousands down to a few hundred, and the measurements appear as dots that join into a new line. Play the dots back: the sound stays itself until the dots get too sparse, then the high parts go first and voices turn muffled and wrong. A second slider sets how many different heights a measurement may take, from thousands down to four, and the sound turns grainy.
takeaway: A recording is a long list of measurements of the air's push taken thousands of times a second, and the sound survives as long as the measurements are frequent and fine enough.
needs: A short sound clip under CC0 (Freesound) for readers who decline the microphone; the microphone path uses the browser's own audio input.
needsSource: none beyond a CC0 clip; sampling and requantising are computed on the page.
pitfall: More measurements per second do not make a sound louder or longer, only truer; the wiggly line is a graph of pressure against time, not a picture of air moving sideways. Do not invoke the sampling theorem by name; show the point where the dots fail.
why: England KS3 computing: data of various types 'including text, sounds and pictures' represented in binary (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study); NGSS MS-PS4-3 on digitized signals (https://www.nextgenscience.org/pe/ms-ps4-3-waves-and-their-applications-technologies-information-transfer).
overlapWith: compression (level 2) uses frequency content to drop detail and fourier-transform decomposes signals; this page stops at measurements, how often and how finely, listened to.

title: Traffic lights that know you are there
interaction: Cars arrive at a crossroads from four directions while a timer runs the lights through a fixed cycle; queues grow on the busy road while the empty road gets its green anyway. Bury a sensor loop in each lane and switch the controller to 'skip a green nobody is waiting for': the queues shrink. Then set the busy road's green longer and shorter and find which choice keeps the total queue smallest.
takeaway: A traffic light is a small counting program, and giving it a sensor so that it can skip empty roads makes the whole crossroads wait less.
needsSource: none; cars arrive at random at set rates and queue, and the loop detector follows the published inductive-loop principle (a metal mass above the loop lowers its inductance and trips the controller).
pitfall: The loop in the road is not a pressure plate: it senses metal, which is why a bicycle may fail to trigger it. Pressing a pedestrian button again does not shorten the wait; the request is registered once.
why: England KS2 computing: 'design, write and debug programs that accomplish specific goals, including controlling or simulating physical systems' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study/national-curriculum-in-england-computing-programmes-of-study); traffic lights are the standard project of the Teach Computing Year 5 physical-computing unit (https://teachcomputing.org/curriculum/key-stage-2/programming-a-selection-in-physical-computing/connecting-crumbles).
overlapWith: feedback-control (level 2) tunes a continuous controller; this one is a rule with a sensor and a timer, with a queue of cars as the cost. graph-search routes one car across a map; this page runs one crossing.

title: Twenty questions: halving the haystack
interaction: Think of a number from 1 to 100 and answer the page's 'higher or lower' questions: a bar of candidates shrinks by half each answer and the counter stops at seven. Now find a word in a thousand-page dictionary by opening it in the middle, then in the middle of the right half, counting the opens, against a search that flips through every page. Then play animal twenty questions: each yes/no question hides half of the hundred animals on the board until one is left.
takeaway: A question that splits what is left in half finds the answer in a handful of steps, where checking one at a time takes hundreds.
needs: The animal board: the UCI Zoo dataset (101 animals, 16 yes/no and count features), CC BY 4.0.
pitfall: Halving only works on a sorted list or on questions that really split the pile: show 'is it a penguin?' barely shrinking the board, and the dictionary trick failing on an unsorted pile of pages.
why: England KS3 computing: 'several key algorithms that reflect computational thinking [for example, ones for sorting and searching]'; CS Unplugged Searching Algorithms ('How many guesses?', 'Divide and conquer', ages 5 to 10). https://www.csunplugged.org/en/topics/searching-algorithms/
overlapWith: sorting (level 1) shows how the cost of sorting grows with input size; nothing in the catalogue shows searching. This page shows halving against one-by-one on counts alone, without growth curves.
needsSource: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Zoo dataset, CC BY 4.0.

title: Databases & queries
interaction: Browse a real table of a few hundred rows, then split it into linked tables with keys so that nothing is stored twice; type a query (filter, sort, join) and watch the rows it touches light up and the result assemble. Turn an index on and off for a search and count the rows examined, then run two edits at once and see why a transaction must either complete or leave no trace.
takeaway: A database keeps each fact once, in tables tied together by keys, and answers questions by combining them, with an index to avoid reading everything.
needs: A small open dataset with natural relations (for instance countries, cities and populations).
needsSource: GeoNames (CC BY 4.0) or the Palmer penguins dataset (CC0)
pitfall: A spreadsheet is not a database: it has no keys, so the same fact can be typed twice and drift apart. An index speeds reading and slows writing; it is not free.
why: OCR A-level Computer Science H446 (relational databases, normalisation to third normal form, SQL) https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/computer-science/ocr/
overlapWith: sorting and graph-search are algorithms on bare arrays and graphs and pagerank builds a web of links; no page shows tables, keys, joins or indexes. The pool's b-trees-transactions (level 3) is the structure of the index and the transaction; this page shows their effect.

title: How a computer plays a game: the search tree
interaction: Play noughts and crosses against the page and open its mind: a tree of the moves it is weighing, the leaves scored win, draw or loss and the scores passed up, the computer taking the best of its moves and assuming you take the worst for it. Switch to Connect Four, where the whole tree is too big, and set how many moves ahead it looks: at two it blunders, at six it is hard to beat, with the count of positions examined rising about sevenfold per extra move; turn on pruning and watch whole branches greyed out with the answer unchanged. Build the scoring rule yourself from a palette of features (centre column, three in a row) and test it.
takeaway: A game-playing program looks ahead down a tree of moves, assumes the opponent plays its best, and picks the line with the best guaranteed outcome; how deep it can afford to look is set by how fast the tree grows.
pitfall: The program does not plan like a person; it counts. And it does not look at every possible game: depth is limited and the leaves are scored by a rule of thumb, which is why a better scoring rule can beat a deeper search.
why: 'How does a chess computer work' tutorials (freeCodeCamp's step-by-step chess AI) are among the most-read introductions to minimax: https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/simple-chess-ai-step-by-step-1d55a9266977
overlapWith: graph-search: searching a map for a route; this page searches a tree of moves against an opponent, where a value flows up instead of a path being found. monte-carlo-tree-search (pool, level 3) uses random playouts and AlphaGo; this page is the full deterministic search at level 1.

title: How a simulation works
interaction: Drop a ball and advance time by hand: each tick the velocity is updated by gravity and the position by the velocity, and the dots trace a path that bends, more smoothly the smaller the step. Make the step too large and the ball tunnels through the floor or an orbiting planet spirals away; compare the stepped path with the exact one and watch the error shrink as the step shrinks, then see that a half-step update holds an orbit that plain stepping loses. Finally open the hood on this site's own pendulum and epidemic pages to find the same loop at work.
takeaway: A simulation is a rule for the next instant applied over and over, so its accuracy is bought with smaller steps and a better update rule, and every animated model on this site is that loop.
pitfall: Smaller steps are not always the fix: a method that gains or loses energy every step (plain Euler on an orbit) drifts however small the step, and the page must show a better update rule curing what a smaller step does not.
why: AP Calculus BC Unit 7, topic 7.5 'Approximating solutions using Euler's method' (slope fields and stepping) https://fiveable.me/ap-calc/unit-7.md ; and the site's own need for a page that explains what every other page is doing
overlapWith: calculus (level 2) shows the derivative as a slope and the integral as an area; this page is their numerical shadow at level 1, and the only page that explains the site's own engine. The pool's numerical-stability (level 3) is the analysis of why methods fail; this page shows them failing. The proposed differential-equations (level 2) draws the slope field and the idea of a rule for the slope; this page is the position-and-velocity update on a ball and an orbit, the engine itself.

title: Random worlds: how games make terrain
interaction: A grid of random arrows and the height map computed from them, drawn as a shaded landscape the reader can tilt; one slider sets how far apart the arrows are, wide for rolling hills, close for rubble. Add layers, each twice as fine and half as tall, and the hills grow ridges, then rocks, with a slider for how fast the layers shrink setting smooth against craggy. Set a sea level to flood the valleys, change the seed for a new world that is different yet looks the same, and compare with plain random numbers per cell, which give static, not land.
takeaway: Natural-looking terrain comes from adding up smooth random bumps at several scales, big for mountains and small for rocks, which is how a game makes an endless world from one seed.
pitfall: This noise is not random in the sense of static: neighbouring points are correlated, which is what makes it look like land. It is not a model of geology, only of its look, and the page should not present it as how mountains form.
why: Minecraft's terrain is layered gradient noise, and 'how is a Minecraft world generated' is a common question (Minecraft Wiki): https://minecraft.fandom.com/wiki/Noise_generator
overlapWith: chaos-fractals: Mandelbrot and self-similar structure found in simple rules; this page builds a deliberately self-similar random landscape and is about generating, not discovering, it.

title: Recursion
interaction: Step through a function that calls itself: the call stack grows as frames are pushed and shrinks as results return, shown beside the code for factorial, the Towers of Hanoi and a tree that draws itself. Count the calls for Fibonacci and watch the call tree explode, switch on memoisation and see it collapse to a line, then remove the base case and watch the stack overflow.
takeaway: A problem that contains smaller copies of itself can be solved by a function that calls itself on the copies, provided it has a smallest case that it answers directly.
pitfall: Recursion is not a loop in disguise: each call is a separate frame with its own variables, which is both why it works and why a missing base case crashes. Naive recursive Fibonacci is slow because it repeats work, not because recursion is slow.
why: OCR A-level Computer Science H446: recursion and stack frames, 'explain recursive techniques, situations when recursion is more useful than iteration' https://denbigh.net/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Year-13-Computer-Science-SOL.pdf
overlapWith: sorting runs merge sort without showing the call stack and chaos-fractals zooms into self-similar sets; this page is the mechanism they share, the stack of frames and the base case.

title: Databases: B-trees & transactions
interaction: Insert and delete keys in a B+tree of adjustable fan-out and watch nodes split and merge, with the disk reads per lookup counted and compared with a binary tree on the same keys. Then run two transactions that interleave on the same rows with a write-ahead log, crash the machine at any point and replay the log to recover, and compare locking with snapshot isolation on an update that each transaction alone would get right.
takeaway: A database keeps rows findable in a handful of disk reads by keeping its tree short and wide, and keeps them correct through a crash by writing its intentions down before acting on them.
pitfall: 'Atomic' means all-or-nothing, not instantaneous, and a transaction is durable once its log record reaches disk, not when the rows are updated; the data pages can be stale at a crash and still be recovered.
why: CMU 15-445 Database Systems, Lecture 08 'B+Tree Index' https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2024/slides/08-trees.pdf
overlapWith: consensus-blockchains: that page replicates one log among machines; this one is a single machine's log and index, and why a tree rather than a chain is what makes lookup fast.

title: Caches & the memory hierarchy
interaction: Choose a program's access pattern (sum an array row by row or column by column, walk a linked list, multiply matrices with and without blocking) and run it through a cache with adjustable size, line length, associativity and replacement policy; each access lights a line as a hit or a miss, and the miss count and the average memory access time plot live. Add a second level of cache and watch where the knee of the curve moves.
takeaway: The same program runs many times faster or slower depending only on whether it touches memory in an order the cache can predict.
pitfall: A bigger cache is not always better: a direct-mapped cache thrashes on a stride equal to its size however large it is, and the unit moved is a whole line, never a byte, so a miss costs the same for one byte as for sixty-four.
why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Unit 14 'Multilevel memories: locality, performance, caches' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar
overlapWith: cpu: that page single-steps instructions against a flat memory that answers instantly; this page makes memory itself the model and shows why one access costs one cycle and the next two hundred.

title: Compilers
interaction: Type a small program in a toy language and step it through the compiler: characters become tokens, tokens a parse tree, the tree an intermediate form, and the intermediate form instructions for the minimal processor of the CPU page, which then runs them. Toggle optimisations (constant folding, dead-code elimination, register allocation by graph colouring) and watch the emitted code shrink and the instruction count fall; introduce a syntax error and see exactly where the parser gives up.
takeaway: A compiler is a chain of mechanical translations, each simple on its own, that turns text a person wrote into instructions a processor can run.
pitfall: A compiler does not understand the program: parsing is a grammar check, and an optimisation may change the code only where it can prove the result is unchanged, which is why it often cannot.
why: Stanford CS143 Compilers (lexical analysis, parsing, code generation, register allocation) https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs143/
overlapWith: cpu: that page runs hand-written assembly; this page shows where the assembly comes from and reuses the same processor so the output actually runs.

title: Pipelines & branch prediction
interaction: Feed a short program into a five-stage pipeline and step it cycle by cycle while instructions overlap in a pipeline diagram; a dependency between neighbouring instructions stalls the pipe until forwarding is switched on. Insert a loop and compare a predictor that always guesses 'not taken' with a two-bit counter, counting the cycles thrown away on each misprediction, then deepen the pipeline and watch that cost grow.
takeaway: A pipelined processor finishes an instruction nearly every cycle only while it can guess what comes next; each wrong guess empties the pipe.
pitfall: Pipelining does not make any single instruction faster; it raises throughput, and a deeper pipeline raises the price of every hazard.
why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Unit 15 'Pipelining the Beta: pipeline diagrams, data hazards' and 'control hazards and exceptions' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar
overlapWith: cpu: that page runs one instruction at a time through fetch, decode and execute; this page overlaps several in flight and shows what breaks when they depend on each other.

title: Dynamic programming
interaction: Watch the recursion tree for the edit distance between two words explode with repeated subproblems, then fill the table cell by cell and trace the cheapest path back to the alignment. Carve seams out of a photo: the page finds the lowest-energy path through the pixel grid with the same table idea and removes it, so the image narrows without squashing its subject; try knapsack with a budget slider.
takeaway: When a problem's subproblems overlap, solving each once and looking it up turns an exponential search into a table that fills in polynomial time.
needs: One CC0 photograph for seam carving (Wikimedia Commons CC0, or a public-domain NASA image).
pitfall: The name has nothing to do with programming or dynamics: it is memoised recursion, and it only works when an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems, which the travelling-salesman problem does not offer in polynomial size.
why: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lectures 15 to 18 'Dynamic Programming' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/calendar
overlapWith: graph-search: Dijkstra's algorithm is a special case; this page makes the table and the overlapping subproblems the object, with seam carving as the visible payoff.
needsSource: one CC0 photo (Wikimedia Commons CC0 or NASA public domain); openly licensed

title: The fast Fourier transform
interaction: Step the recursion on 8, 16 or 64 samples: split even and odd, recurse, and combine with twiddle factors drawn as rotations on the unit circle, in a butterfly diagram that grows with n. Count the multiplications against the direct transform as n doubles, then use the result to multiply two long polynomials (or two big integers) and watch the product appear in n log n steps.
takeaway: The Fourier transform of n samples takes n squared steps done directly, but the two halves of the problem share nearly all their work, and reusing it brings the cost down to n log n.
pitfall: The FFT is not an approximation or a different transform: it computes exactly the discrete Fourier transform, only faster, and it needs evenly spaced samples.
why: MIT 6.046J Design and Analysis of Algorithms, Lecture 3 'Divide & Conquer: FFT' (Demaine: 'probably the most taught algorithm at MIT') https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-046j-design-and-analysis-of-algorithms-spring-2015/resources/lecture-3-divide-conquer-fft/
overlapWith: fourier-transform: that page shows what the transform means; this one shows how to compute it fast, and the counting of operations is the graphic.

title: Floating point
interaction: Zoom along the number line and watch the representable numbers thin out away from zero, with the bits of the selected value shown; type 0.1 + 0.2 and see where each operand lands and why the sum misses 0.3 by one unit in the last place. Subtract two nearly equal numbers and watch the significant digits vanish, sum a million small numbers in two orders and compare, then switch on compensated summation; run the same calculation in half, single and double precision.
takeaway: A floating-point number is the nearest representable value, not the number itself, and the gap between neighbours grows with size, so the order of operations changes the answer.
pitfall: Floating-point arithmetic is not random or buggy: each operation is correctly rounded and its error is predictable from the exponent; the trouble is accumulation and cancellation, not the single operation.
why: Computerphile 'Floating Point Numbers', about 2.5 million views (view count from aggregator snapshots found this session; the video id is recalled, not fetched this session) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZRI1IfStY0
overlapWith: binary: that page reads one bit pattern as a float; this page explores the gaps between floats and what they do to arithmetic.

title: Garbage collection
interaction: Run a small program that allocates objects and drops references, shown as a heap of boxes with pointers; press collect and watch mark-and-sweep trace from the roots and free what it never reached, then switch to a copying collector that compacts the survivors and to a generational one that collects only the nursery most of the time. Tune the heap size and watch pause length and memory use trade against each other; build a cycle of objects and see reference counting leak it.
takeaway: A collector never knows what the program will need; it keeps whatever is still reachable from the running program and reclaims everything else.
pitfall: Reference counting is not the whole story: it cannot free cycles, and 'the program is done with this object' is undecidable in general, so reachability is the proxy every collector uses.
why: UC Berkeley CS61B, Lecture 39 'Garbage collection' (mark-sweep, copying, generational) https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs61b/fa17/materials/lectures/lect39.pdf
overlapWith: graph-search: marking is a graph traversal; graph-search finds a path, this page uses the traversal to decide what memory can be thrown away and shows the pauses it costs.

title: Hash tables & Bloom filters
interaction: Insert keys into a table with chaining or open addressing and raise the load factor; every probe is drawn, and the measured mean probe length is plotted against the expected curve until the table resizes and rehashes. Then feed the same keys to a Bloom filter with an adjustable bit array and number of hash functions, query keys that were never inserted and watch the measured false-positive rate track the formula; degrade the hash function with a slider and see both structures cluster.
takeaway: A good hash spreads keys evenly, so lookups stay constant-time until the table fills, and a Bloom filter trades a known, tunable false-positive rate for a fraction of the memory.
pitfall: A hash table's constant time is an average under a good hash, not a guarantee; the cryptographic hash of the cryptography page is a different tool; and a Bloom filter can only ever say 'definitely absent', never 'definitely present'.
why: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 4 'Hashing' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes (Bloom filters appear in CMU 15-445's index lectures)
overlapWith: cryptography: that page shows a hash as a one-way fingerprint; here the hash is a fast bucket index, and the model is the statistics of collisions as the table fills.
